prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of the time-reversal-invariant topological insulator and quantum spin Hall effect, and for the first experimental observation of the quantum spin Hall state.

statement.case_for: I maintain B004 as my first choice after reading all eight opening ballots. Seven of eight members place it in their top three, which is the broadest top-rank agreement on the shortlist, but I rest the case on the physics rather than the count. Kane and Mele showed that time-reversal symmetry plus spin-orbit coupling gives a Z2 invariant and protected helical edge states without any magnetic field, and Molenkamp's group then observed the predicted edge conduction in HgTe quantum wells. A sharp, testable prediction followed by a clean experimental confirmation is the pattern a discovery prize should reward. The interpretation has been stable for roughly fifteen to twenty years, with independent transport and ARPES confirmation across 2D and 3D materials, and the idea reorganised how band structures are classified and searched. The three credited names map onto a coherent theory-plus-experiment prize without needing the cap to cut anyone arbitrarily, which is not true of B002, B023 or B021.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution at the boundary of the discovery. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang made the HgTe proposal that Molenkamp's group tested, Zhang is deceased, and 3D topological insulator work (Fu-Kane-Mele, Moore-Balents, Hasan, Shen) sits outside the credited names. A citation must therefore be drawn tightly around the Z2 quantum spin Hall prediction and its first observation. A second concern is overlap with the 2016 prize on topological phases and phase transitions; I think the physics is distinct (symmetry-protected, no quantised Hall conductance from a field, time-reversal classification) but a colleague could fairly argue for letting the field mature further before a second topological prize.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks B043 first on the strength of the IceCube diffuse flux and source evidence, and places B004 third, noting that BHZ and Zhang are missing from the credit and that overlap with 2016 may weigh against it.
responses.response: I take the BHZ gap seriously and it is why I would write the citation around Kane and Mele's Z2 prediction and the first observation, not around HgTe design. I do not think it disqualifies the trio, because the committee has to credit a discovery, and Kane-Mele is the decisive conceptual step. On B043, I respect the opening of a new window, but Danielsson himself says source identification still rests on a few associations and Eva Lindroth and Eva Olsson both rank it last on their ballots for related reasons. I would rather wait for the astrophysical source picture, with KM3NeT cross-checks, to firm up than give a prize on leadership credit for a collaboration of thousands.

responses.point: Mehlig puts B009 first as a clean theory-experiment pair, with correlated insulators and superconductivity from geometry, and B004 second, calling it timely and arguably overdue.
responses.response: I agree with the quality of the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction, and I rank B009 fourth only because of maturity, not merit. Your own opening says the superconducting mechanism is debated and a citation would have to be framed around flat-band correlated physics; that is a narrower citation than B004 needs. The experimental credit also leaves out the lead student of the 2018 papers and parallel groups. I would put B009 as my first alternative if the committee wants a newer field, but I would still favour the more settled topological result now, and B009 gains from a few more years of resolution on pairing and sample dependence.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B006 first as a clean, mature two-person measurement prize, and places B004 third with the BHZ credit gap as the open question. He also declares a research stay in the Hall laboratory milieu from which Ye emerged.
responses.response: I agree B006 is the cleanest allocation on the list and I rank it second; Katori's magic-wavelength idea and Ye's 10^-18 systematics are unambiguous and widely reproduced. My hesitation is conceptual novelty: the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize cover adjacent ground, and I weigh a new organising principle in quantum matter above a further step in precision. Kroll's disclosed Hall-lab connection is fairly flagged and does not weaken his technical argument, but it is one reason the committee should not let B006 pass on his and Eva Lindroth's rank-one support without a separate check of Ye's credit relative to the comb lineage.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B004 first, valuing the Z2 insight as having reshaped band-structure computation and search, while noting that BHZ and 3D credit are outside the names and that he cannot verify priority.
responses.response: I agree and add a point from my own field: the Z2 classification mattered because it was an invariant one could compute and test, which is what let theory guide materials. Where I would press back is the weight on 3D generalisation. Including 3D topological insulators in the citation would push beyond the credited names and make the allocation harder, so I prefer a narrow citation on the quantum spin Hall effect and its observation, and leaving 3D to be recognised, if at all, as a separate matter.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, ranks B002 first, arguing that the Higgs observation remains unrecognised experimentally while the 2013 theory prize is done, and that the three-person limit forces a choice among founders and spokespersons.
responses.response: I do not question that the Higgs discovery is among the most important experimental results of the era, and I ranked it sixth only because of the attribution problem that Pearce himself calls a genuine judgement call. Four credited names for three seats, two collaborations of thousands, and a choice between founders and announcement-time spokespersons that nobody on the committee can resolve from the supplied text, means a prize would be contested whatever we choose. Eriksson and Kroll both land on Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee while I leaned toward including Gianotti, which shows how unsettled the choice is even among members who agree on the candidate, but I would want the committee to settle the principle before choosing. I rank B004 above it because its credit is cleaner, not because its science is more important.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts a Kane-Mele-Molenkamp citation limited to the Z2 quantum spin Hall effect without Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, or whether the omission is treated as disqualifying.
How much weight the 2016 topological-phases prize should carry as a timing or overlap objection, given that members Danielsson, Mehlig, Olsson and Pearce raise it.
Whether B009 has matured enough on the superconducting mechanism and experimental credit to overtake B004 in a later round.
How to settle the Higgs credit principle (founders versus spokespersons) well enough that B002 could be compared fairly on the physics.
Whether any fairer way exists to treat B006 given prior comb and ion-clock recognition.
statement.conflict_note: I work in superconducting circuits and quantum computing, so I have a clear field and institutional connection to B015 (circuit QED): I direct WACQT at Chalmers, collaborate with Chalmers colleagues Delsing and Wilson and with Anton Frisk Kockum, and Chalmers hosted researchers associated with the 2025 prize. I would recuse myself from deliberating on B015. No specific personal or institutional connection to B004, B006, B009 or the other shortlisted candidates is apparent from the provided profile.
